content.text:
If you’re in the **United States**, you probably **can’t realistically buy a Japanese dwarf flying squirrel** (*Pteromys momonga*) as a normal pet. They’re native to Japan, uncommon in the pet trade, and may be protected/regulated. I’d be very skeptical of any “Japanese dwarf flying squirrel for sale” listing online—many are scams or misidentified animals.

What you can do instead:

1. **Check your state wildlife/exotic pet laws first.** Flying squirrel rules vary a lot by state and sometimes city/county. Some states ban them; others require permits.
2. **Contact your state fish & wildlife agency** and ask specifically about *Pteromys momonga* and/or non-native flying squirrels.
3. **If legal where you live, look for USDA-licensed exotic animal breeders**—but in the U.S. the species usually sold, where legal, is the **southern flying squirrel** (*Glaucomys volans*), not the Japanese dwarf flying squirrel. Reputable sellers should provide a USDA license number, captive-bred documentation, and health records. ([legalclarity.org](https://legalclarity.org/is-it-legal-to-own-a-flying-squirrel/?utm_source=openai))
4. **Do not import one yourself** without professional help and permits. U.S. Fish & Wildlife regulates imports/exports of wildlife, and live wild mammals have declaration/import requirements; state law can be stricter. ([fws.gov](https://www.fws.gov/program/office-of-law-enforcement/information-importers-exporters?utm_source=openai))

Also note: the Japanese dwarf flying squirrel is endemic to Japan and is reported as endangered in many Japanese prefectures, so ethical/legal sourcing is a major concern. ([ffpri.go.jp](https://www.ffpri.go.jp/ffpri/en/research/results/2023/documents/20230215press.pdf?utm_source=openai))

If you tell me your **state/city**, I can help you figure out whether any flying squirrel is legal there and what agency/permit to check.
